title: Deep Learning and Neural Networks
topicSummary: Neural architectures, activation functions, backpropagation, CNN, time series modeling (LSTM) etc., Case studies.

content.text: 1. Overview
This module advances from classical ML (Week 6–8) to Deep Learning for complex pattern recognition and sequential predictions.
2. What are Neural Networks?
Definition: A Neural Network is a computational model inspired by the brain, consisting of interconnected nodes (neurons).
Basic Structure:
Mathematical Representation: y = f(Wx + b) where W is weights, b is bias, and f is the activation function.

📖 Reading Note: A biological analogy helps: a single neuron in the brain receives signals from other neurons (dendrites = inputs), processes them (cell body = weighted sum + bias), and fires an output signal if stimulated strongly enough (axon = activation function output). A neural network with millions of these artificial neurons stacked in layers can recognize faces, understand speech, and predict city traffic — all learned purely from data. The more hidden layers, the 'deeper' the network — hence 'Deep Learning'.
3. Neural Architectures
👉 Key Idea: More layers allow learning of complex, nonlinear relationships.
4. Activation Functions
Definition: Introduce non-linearity to allow learning of complex patterns.

📖 Reading Note: Why ReLU replaced Sigmoid as the default? The 'vanishing gradient problem'. Sigmoid squashes all inputs into (0,1); for very large or small inputs, gradients become nearly zero, so the network stops learning in early layers during backpropagation. ReLU (f(x)=max(0,x)) avoids this — gradients flow cleanly for positive values. In urban deep learning models (e.g., vehicle detection CNN for Indian roads), using ReLU consistently outperforms Sigmoid by 8-15% accuracy because ReLU allows much deeper networks to train effectively.
5. Backpropagation
Definition: The algorithm used to train neural networks by updating weights using gradient descent to minimize error.
Process: Forward pass → Calculate error → Backward pass (compute gradients) → Update weights.
Error Function Example: L = ½(y - ŷ)²

📖 Reading Note: Backpropagation works by the chain rule of calculus — computing how much each weight contributed to the total error, layer by layer from output back to input. Think of it as 'blaming' each neuron for its share of the error, then adjusting it. An epoch is one complete pass through all training data (forward + backward). Training a pollution prediction DNN on 2 years of hourly data might require 100 epochs — the model progressively corrects itself 100 times. Batch size (how many samples per update) also matters: smaller batches = noisier but faster convergence; larger batches = smoother but needs more memory.
6. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
Definition: Specialized for image and spatial data processing.
Components:
Convolution layers, Pooling layers, Fully connected layers.
Applications:
Traffic camera analysis, Vehicle detection, Crowd monitoring.

📖 Reading Note: How a CNN analyzes a traffic camera image: (1) Convolution layers apply small 'filters' (3x3 or 5x5 pixel windows) that slide across the image, detecting edges, corners, and shapes. (2) Pooling layers shrink the feature maps (e.g., from 224x224 to 112x112) retaining dominant features — reducing computation. (3) Fully connected layers combine all detected features to classify: 'This image contains 12 cars, 3 trucks, 1 auto-rickshaw.' Pretrained CNNs like ResNet-50 (trained on 14 million images) are fine-tuned on local traffic camera datasets — this transfer learning approach reduces training time from weeks to hours.
7. Time Series Modeling (LSTM)
Definition: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a type of RNN used for sequential/time-dependent data.
Why LSTM?
Captures long-term dependencies that traditional models miss.
Key Gates:
Forget gate, Input gate, Output gate.
Applications:
Traffic prediction over time, Weather forecasting, Energy demand prediction.

📖 Reading Note: LSTM's three gates control what the network 'remembers': Forget gate decides which past information to discard (e.g., yesterday's traffic at 2am is irrelevant to predict today's 8am peak). Input gate decides what new information to store (e.g., today is a Monday — a strong pattern feature). Output gate decides what to output (e.g., predict next hour's traffic volume). In Delhi Metro's demand prediction system, an LSTM model uses 7 days of hourly ridership as input sequence. The forget gate learns to ignore non-weekday patterns on Mondays — the network automatically discovers weekly seasonality without being explicitly programmed to.
8. Deep Learning Workflow
Data collection → Preprocessing → Model selection (CNN, LSTM) → Training (backpropagation) → Evaluation → Deployment.
9. Case Studies (Urban Applications)

items: Case Study 1 (Traffic Monitoring): CNN analyzes camera images for vehicle count.
Case Study 2 (Traffic Forecasting): LSTM uses historical data for future congestion prediction.
Case Study 3 (Crowd Density): DNN estimates population density.

content.text: 10. Challenges in Deep Learning

rows: "Black box" nature; hard to explain decisions

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: The 'black box' interpretability problem is a real governance challenge in smart cities. When a deep learning model recommends demolishing a building as 'structural risk', city officials need to justify the decision to affected residents. Tools like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) help explain individual predictions from any ML/DL model. For Bengaluru's storm drain overflow prediction DNN, using SHAP revealed that 'rainfall intensity in the previous 2 hours' was the single most influential feature — helping engineers understand and trust the model's recommendations.
11. Topic Connections
How Week 9 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: Neural networks use the same gradient descent and loss functions introduced in Week 6 — deep learning is just more layers of the same principle
Backpropagation IS gradient descent applied layer-by-layer — it is the practical implementation of Week 6's optimization theory inside a network
Activation functions determine the non-linearity of the model — they are the critical design choice in model building that distinguishes deep models from simple linear models
IoT cameras (Week 10–11) generate raw image streams; CNN models (Week 9) are deployed on the microcontroller or edge device to process those images in real-time
Dynamic data (live traffic, weather — introduced in Week 2 as a data type) is exactly what LSTM models are built to predict — closing the loop between data types and algorithms
The challenges (interpretability, data needs, computation) discussed in Week 9 directly inform the design tradeoffs in Week 12's integrated smart city platforms

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 9 is the technical peak of the ML section (Weeks 6–9). CNN and LSTM are the two DL models most useful in urban informatics — CNN for spatial/image data from cameras, LSTM for temporal/time-series data from sensors. After Week 9, the course shifts from algorithms to deployment (Weeks 10–12) — asking 'how do we put this intelligence into the real city?'
